name: Hueyatlaco
hook: Stone tools near Puebla dated to 245,000+ years by two methods — a date even the excavator rejected.
claim: Bifacial and unifacial tools, including a Lerma-style point, were excavated with extinct fauna at Hueyatlaco. U-series dating of a camel pelvis and fission-track dating of nearby tephra placed the tool beds at ~245,000-600,000 years, far older than any accepted evidence of people in the Americas.

claimed_age.label: ~245,000 yr (U-series); tephra to ~600,000 yr (FT)
claimed_age.basis: 230Th (245,000±40,000 yr) on a camel pelvis with bifacial tools (Szabo et al. 1969). Overlying tephra gave FT ages of 370,000±200,000 and 600,000±340,000 yr, deemed compatible (Steen-McIntyre 1981). Calendar years.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: Clovis-first: no secure evidence of people in the Americas older than about 11,500 radiocarbon years (the 'Clovis barrier').

unambiguous_signal.note: Bifaces, unifacial scrapers and a Lerma-style point are accepted as genuine worked stone tools; the dispute is over their age, not their manufacture.

documented_context.note: Multi-year excavation mapped a detailed stratigraphic section, but later work flagged shifting channels and an unconformity in the tool-bearing unit that could indicate reworked material.

multiple_dating_methods.note: U-series on bone and zircon fission-track on tephra gave broadly compatible old ages, though critics say the two fission-track dates are in reverse stratigraphic order.

multiple_labs.note: Sources reviewed do not specify whether U-series and fission-track work were run at separate laboratories.

professional_recovery.note: Excavated by archaeologist Cynthia Irwin-Williams; the in situ artifact-fauna association was independently confirmed in print by three other named archaeologists in 1969.

peer_reviewed_report.note: Initial dating paper appeared in Earth and Planetary Science Letters the same year as the claim; the full geological report followed 12 years later, in 1981.

material_accessible.note: Independent biostratigraphers sampled sediment in the region for decades afterward, but accessibility of the original dated bone specimens to critics is not confirmed in sources reviewed.

independent_teams.note: Three outside archaeologists independently verified the field association within the claim year, but no independent lab replicated the dates within about five years.

proponent_stake.note: No commercial, religious or nationalist motive is documented in sources reviewed; all named researchers had ordinary academic or government-geologist affiliations.

objections.text: The extreme ages are inconsistent with the tools' typology: bifaces and a Lerma-style point of this form are not otherwise known from anywhere near this age.
objections.outcome_note: Malde and Steen-McIntyre replied in the same 1981 issue that typology cannot override concordant physical dates; no resolution followed.

objections.text: U-series dates on bone are vulnerable to contamination and open-system uranium behavior after burial, so the camel-pelvis date may not reflect true burial age.
objections.outcome_note: No independent re-dating of the specific specimen has been reported to confirm or rule out contamination.

objections.text: The two fission-track dates on zircon from the tephra units are in reverse stratigraphic order, undermining confidence in the dating sequence.
objections.outcome_note: The original authors' stratigraphic account addresses the section in detail, but the apparent reversal has not been independently re-examined since.

objections.text: Older fossils may have been reworked (redeposited) from earlier deposits into the younger archaeological levels, explaining old bone dates without requiring ancient tool use.
objections.outcome_note: Pichardo proposes this mechanism and separately dates the Lerma-point level to about 14,000-16,000 BP on biostratigraphic and radiocarbon grounds, but it has not been tested directly on the dated specimens.

objections.text: A 250,000+ year human presence in the Americas has no corroborating fossil, archaeological or genetic trace elsewhere in the Americas or in northeast Asia.
objections.outcome_note: No site of comparable age has been reported anywhere in the Americas in the decades since; the controversy remains confined to Valsequillo.

objections.text: The old ages rest on very few dated specimens tied to the tool levels (essentially one camel pelvis and one mastodon molar), too small a sample to be conclusive.
objections.outcome_note: Pichardo notes the same small-sample criticism, often leveled at younger dates nearby at Caulapan, applies symmetrically to the old Hueyatlaco and El Horno dates.

status_note: No consensus age exists. The U-series and fission-track dates are neither replicated nor refuted, and no mundane cause (contamination, reworking) is confirmed. Most archaeologists reject the extreme ages; the case is not formally settled.

timeline.event: Szabo, Malde and Irwin-Williams report U-series dates of ~245,000 years on a camel pelvis found with bifacial tools, calling it a 'dilemma'.
Independent archaeologists MacNeish, Petersen and Wormington confirm the in situ artifact-fauna association in print.
Field team retraces the stratigraphic section at Hueyatlaco during further excavation to confirm bed relationships.
Steen-McIntyre, Fryxell and Malde publish the full geological case, adding fission-track dates up to ~600,000 years on overlying tephra.
Irwin-Williams publishes a commentary in the same journal rejecting the ages as incompatible with tool typology; Malde and Steen-McIntyre reply.
Pichardo proposes, from independent biostratigraphy, that redeposited older fossils explain the anomalous dates and that the tools are much younger.
Pichardo argues from regional radiocarbon and tephra work that the tool horizon dates to ~14,000-16,000 BP, far younger than the U-series/fission-track figures.
VanLandingham argues from diatom biostratigraphy for a Sangamonian-age (roughly 130,000-80,000 yr) correlation for Valsequillo artifacts.
Gonzalez, Huddart and Bennett review the Valsequillo dating disputes, including Hueyatlaco, and describe the age question as still unresolved.
VanLandingham instead argues for an older, Yarmouthian correlation (~430,000-500,000 yr), diverging from the 2004 estimate for the same site.

decisive_tests.test: Independently re-date the original camel-pelvis and mastodon-molar specimens (if still curated) by U-series at a second laboratory, cross-checked by a second method such as ESR on the same bone.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the ~245,000-280,000-year bone ages replicate outside the original USGS work, or reflect post-burial uranium uptake.

decisive_tests.test: Re-examine in the field whether the tool-bearing beds and dated tephra are in clean primary position or are cut by channels and unconformities suggesting redeposition.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the association between tools and 245,000+-year sediments is primary context or a mixed, reworked one.

decisive_tests.test: Apply modern single-crystal 40Ar/39Ar or (U-Th)/He dating to the tephra units, independent of the 1970s zircon fission-track work.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether modern geochronology reproduces fission-track ages of 370,000-600,000 years for the same tephra.

decisive_tests.test: Commission a blind, independent diatom biostratigraphy study of the same beds to test VanLandingham's conflicting 2004 and 2010 age estimates.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether an independent analyst reproduces either VanLandingham estimate, or neither.

falsifier: Refuted as an ancient site if re-dating finds contamination or open-system uranium behavior inflating the U-series ages, or if re-examination shows the tools lie in redeposited sediment. Strengthened if independent labs replicate the ages and rule out redeposition.

confidence_note: The 1969-1981 exchange is only partly readable: S2, S5 checked via abstracts, S8 checked in full, but S1, S3, S4 are metadata-only (blocked). Later work (S9, S10) is thin and self-inconsistent.
corrections: Brief: dates '~250,000 years from uranium-series ... and tephra/geology'. Confirmed for U-series, but the 1981 paper also reports FT ages to 600,000±340,000 years, called compatible -- wider than '~250,000 years' alone (S2).

Brief: dates 'far older than excavator expected ... conflict ... never resolved'. Undersells Irwin-Williams: co-authored the 1969 paper, then in 1981 rejected the ages as incompatible with tool typology -- proponent and critic (S3, via S8).
notes: Distinct from the Valsequillo footprints in the Xalnene Tuff at Cerro Toluquilla, a separate find and dispute (S6 reviews both, not conflated here; Renne 2005 and Feinberg 2009 on footprints were located but excluded as out of scope). independent_methods_count (2) counts U-series and fission-track as independent quantitative methods; hydration and mineral etching are qualitative support only. Juan Armenta Camacho is credited in popular accounts with finding Valsequillo material before Irwin-Williams's dig: UNVERIFIED this session.
